KAFKA-20901: Enforce cordoned log directories configured with relative paths (#23241)

Kafka allows `log.dirs `to be configured with relative paths, but
`cordoned.log.dirs` was validated and applied using the original
configuration strings, whereas `LogManager` converts log directories to
absolute paths and uses those paths for directory ID lookups.

As a result, configuring `cordoned.log.dirs` with the absolute path
reported by `DescribeLogDirs` was rejected when `log.dirs` contained the
equivalent relative path. Using the relative path passed validation, but
it did not match the absolute path used internally, so the directory was
not reported as cordoned to the controller.

This change consistently uses absolute paths when validating and
applying `cordoned.log.dirs`, including during dynamic reconfiguration
and broker heartbeat propagation.

Reviewers: Mickael Maison <mickael.maison@gmail.com>

MINOR: Derive SSL principal from the matched groups in SslPrincipalMapper (#24010)

SslPrincipalMapper.Rule.apply checks the rule with Matcher.matches() but
then builds the principal with String.replaceAll, which scans the DN
again and can use a different match. For some rules (unanchored, or with
alternation) this gives a wrong name, e.g. "bobeng" instead of "bob", or
the replacement applied twice.

Build the name from the same match with Matcher.appendReplacement. A
rule that produces an empty name is now treated as not matching, so the
next rule applies, the same way an invalid result is handled for
Kerberos rules.

Added unit tests in SslPrincipalMapperTest.

Reviewers: Manikumar Reddy <manikumar@confluent.io>

MINOR: Fix race in StreamsGroupWarmupTaskIntegrationTest (#23944)

The test sampled the thread metadata for a standby task to detect the
warm-up. The metadata shows it only until the promotion, so a test
thread stalled for about two heartbeat intervals missed it and timed
out. Record the warm-up's start and its promotion through a
StandbyUpdateListener instead.

KAFKA-21214: Start the new map of a member at the default capacity (follow-up) (#24001)

A member that owns no partitions gets its new map from
`Utils.newHashMap(0)` in `AssignmentBuilder.ownedPartitions`. Its table
starts with a single slot and resizes at 1, 2, 4 and 7 entries before
reaching the default capacity of 16. This patch sizes the map for at
least 12 entries, which a map of the default capacity holds without
resizing.

KAFKA-20866: Remove incremental-only append result state (#23749)

RecordAppendResult is created for every successful append. This change
removes the incremental-strategy-only outcome and extensionBytesNeeded
fields from regular results. Buffer-extension capacity is now held only
by a private result subtype, while the existing append/new-batch
behavior remains unchanged.

The chunked accumulator consumes the capacity through a package-private
accessor, and a regression test covers the buffer-extension result
contract.

KAFKA-16304: Report file read errors from SslTransportLayer.transferFrom as such (#23928)

Follow-up to #23445, under the same ticket (resolved, fix version
4.5.0).

Since #23445, a failed send of fetched records is passed to a handler
that re-reads the region on the scheduler, and the log directory is
offlined only if the re-read fails too. The re-read is needed because
over PLAINTEXT `sendfile` reads the file and writes the socket in one
call, so a disk error and a socket error are the same bare
`IOException`. `SslTransportLayer.transferFrom` does not have that
problem: it reads the file with `FileChannel.read`, then encrypts and
writes, so it knows which of the two failed. As discussed on #23445,
this passes that on instead of finding it out again:

* `SslTransportLayer.transferFrom` throws a new `FileReadException`, an
  `IOException` with the position of the read, when `FileChannel.read`
  or `FileChannel.size` fails. A `ClosedChannelException`, from a
  deletion or a shutdown, is rethrown as is
  (`FileReadException.ofReadFailure`).
* `TransferableChannel.distinguishesFileReadFailures()` says whether a
  transport does that: true for TLS, false, the default, for
  PLAINTEXT.
* `FileRecords.writeTo` passes to the handler a `FileReadException`
  always, a `ClosedChannelException` never, and any other
  `IOException` only if the transport cannot tell a failed read of the
  file from a failed write to the network channel. A failure of its own
  `channel.size()` call before the transfer becomes a
  `FileReadException` as well, unless it is a `ClosedChannelException`.
* `LocalLog` reports a `FileReadException` as a failure of the log
  directory right away, without re-reading the region. Other failures
  are re-read on the scheduler as before.
* `LogDirFailureChannel.maybeAddOfflineLogDir` logs the error only when
  it takes the log directory offline, so that the failures that follow
  in a failing directory do not flood the log.

Consequences worth stating:

* On TLS listeners a disconnect no longer re-reads the region that was
  being sent. In the test notes, consumers killed mid-fetch over TLS
  for 5 minutes made the scheduler re-read 151 MB without this change
  and nothing with it.
* On TLS listeners a read error now offlines the log directory even if
  the region could be read again by the time of a re-read, e.g. after a
  transient media error. Before, such an error was attributed to the
  socket. This is the criterion `LocalLog` applies to any other
  `IOException`.
* A failed `FileChannel.size()` call on the segment, over either
  transport, is now reported as a read failure without a re-read.
* For every caller of `maybeAddOfflineLogDir`, an error in a log
  directory that is already offline is no longer logged there.
* PLAINTEXT listeners still re-read: `sendfile` cannot tell the two
  apart.
* KRaft snapshots, sent through `UnalignedFileRecords`, are still not
  covered.

KAFKA-21214: [8/8] Add the uniform2 consumer group assignor (#23723)

The uniform assignor balances the total number of partitions per member
but not the partitions of each topic: with homogeneous subscriptions, a
member can get all the partitions of a topic while the others get none
of them. The throughput is usually about the same across the partitions
of a topic but not across topics, so adding members does not spread the
load.

This patch adds uniform2, the next version of the uniform assignor, from
the steps of the previous patches. It lives next to the uniform assignor
while it is developed and is not registered as a built-in assignor. Its
assignments have these properties, in priority order:
- Every partition of every subscribed topic goes to exactly one of its
  subscribers.
- Every subscriber of a topic gets the same number of its partitions,
  the minimum quota, or one more, with an extra partition.
- No extra partition could move to another subscriber of its topic
  whose assignment is at least two partitions smaller.
- Partitions stay with their owners where the above allows. The
  placement moves the fewest partitions for the quotas, and an
  assignment that already has these properties is returned unchanged.
- The result is deterministic.

Changes:
- `Uniform2Assignor` and `AssignmentBuilder`, which reads the group,
  runs the `KeepStickyExtraPartitions`, `AssignRemainingExtraPartitions`
  and `BalanceExtraPartitions` steps on the quotas, places every topic
  and builds the result. Partitions of topics that a member does not
  subscribe to or which no longer exist are dropped. The class Javadoc
  of `Uniform2Assignor` describes the steps with a worked example.
- The result reuses the maps and sets of the members that do not change.
  `RangeSet` becomes public to return consecutive partitions.
- The assignor does not use racks yet. Rack awareness comes in a later
  patch.
- `ConsumerAssignorBenchmark` gets `UNIFORM2`.
- End to end tests with hand traced expectations, written with the group
  spec and topics fixtures, and a shared checker of the properties.

KAFKA-21356: Relieve the persister thread of share group DLQ processing. (#23964)

Copying records into the DLQ was dominated by work on the persister
thread, which also completes write responses for every share partition:

- isDlqEnabledOnTopic and dlqTopicMaxMessageBytes built a LogConfig,
which parses every topic config, on each DLQ request. Read the one key
directly. (Affects both copy on and off case)
- The source record read of ran synchronously on the persister thread.
Run it (and later rounds) on a single-threaded fetch executor owned and
shut down by BrokerServer. (Affects copy on case)
- ShareGroupDLQRecordFetcher.collectRecords visited every batch of a 1
MiB log read, loading each file-backed batch from disk, although a
request wants a few records. We can simply reject batches where the
batch baseOffset > dlq endoffset (V2 only, Affects copy on case).

KAFKA-21193: Speed up SuppressionIntegrationTest and JoinStoreIntegrationTest (#23655)

Six of the 14 cases in SuppressionIntegrationTest take 42 to 46 seconds
each. Each test method uses a fixed application id, so the
withHeaders=false and withHeaders=true runs share one consumer group,
and the second run waits until the previous member's session times out.
shouldUseDefaultSerdes also reused the "-shouldInheritSerdes" test id,
so it shared a group and topics with shouldInheritSerdes. The two
shouldShutdownWhen... tests were not affected, because their members
send a LeaveGroup when the stream thread fails.

This uses safeUniqueTestName(testInfo) for the test id, as #23594 did
for FineGrainedAutoResetIntegrationTest, so every run gets its own
application id and topics. The changelog topic names checked in
shouldAllowOverridingChangelogConfig and shouldCreateChangelogByDefault
were hard-coded with the old application id, so they are now built from
the application id.

JoinStoreIntegrationTest has the same issue: each of its two
parameterized tests reuses an application id across invocations, so the
withHeaders=true invocation waits about 45 seconds for the previous
member's session to time out. Both tests now use
safeUniqueTestName(testInfo) to give each invocation its own application
id. The changelog topic names checked in
streamJoinChangelogTopicShouldBeConfiguredWithDeleteOnlyCleanupPolicy
are now built from that id. Locally, the class went from 94.9s to 6.9s.

Local runs of SuppressionIntegrationTest on the same machine (1 run
before, 3 runs after):

- Test time: 289s before, 32.4 to 32.5s after
- Cases over 30s: 6 before, 0 after
- Result: 14 passed before and after

KAFKA-21349: Wait for the high watermark before loading transaction metadata (#23943)

When a broker becomes the leader of a `__transaction_state` partition,
`TransactionStateManager` loads the log up to the log end offset. A
newly elected leader can have records above the high watermark that are
not committed yet and can still be truncated if leadership moves again,
even with clean elections. The coordinator then acts on state that is
later rolled back. For example, it can send COMMIT markers for a
PREPARE_COMMIT that the next leader doesn't have, and that leader later
times out and aborts the transaction, so the transaction is committed on
some partitions and aborted on others.

Loading with `FetchIsolation.HIGH_WATERMARK` is not enough, because a
new leader's high watermark can lag behind the true one, so the load
would miss committed records.

The coordinator doesn't write to the partition while it is loading
(requests get `COORDINATOR_LOAD_IN_PROGRESS`), so the log end offset at
the start of the load doesn't change. Once the high watermark reaches
it, every record the load reads is committed. This change:

- In `loadTransactionsForTxnTopicPartition`, if the high watermark is
below the log end offset, registers a `PartitionListener` and schedules
the load once the high watermark reaches the log end offset. The high
watermark is checked again after the listener is added, since an update
between reading it and adding the listener isn't delivered to the
listener.
- Abandons the load (removes the `loadingPartitions` entry) if the
partition is not online, becomes a follower, fails or is deleted before
the high watermark catches up. This runs on the scheduler, since
listeners are invoked with partition locks held.
- Skips partitions that are loading in
`removeExpiredTransactionalIds()`. On a leader epoch bump, the previous
epoch's cache entry stays until the new load replaces it, and tombstones
written for it would move the log end offset while the load waits.
- Logs the time spent waiting for the high watermark as part of the load
time.

In the normal case the wait is about one follower fetch round trip. If
an ISR follower is unavailable, the load waits until it is removed from
the ISR (`replica.lag.time.max.ms`). This does not cover unclean leader
election, where committed records can be lost.

Testing: added unit tests to `TransactionStateManagerTest` for waiting
for the high watermark, abandoning on each partition transition and when
the partition is not online, the high watermark advancing during
listener registration, a leader epoch bump while waiting, and expiration
of a partition that is being reloaded.

MINOR: Use Locale.ROOT for the SCRAM iteration count and remove the unused credential string format (#23909)

`ScramMessages.ServerFirstMessage.toMessage()` builds the SCRAM
server-first-message with `String.format("r=%s,s=%s,i=%d", ...)`.
Without an explicit `Locale`, `%d` follows the JVM's default locale, and
on a broker whose default locale uses native digits (for example
`ar-EG`, `fa-IR`, `bn-BD`, `ne-NP`; JDK 9+ CLDR data) the iteration
count is emitted as `i=٤٠٩٦` instead of `i=4096`.

RFC 5802 requires ASCII digits, and `ServerFirstMessage` itself parses
the count with `i=(?<iterations>[0-9]+)`, so every SCRAM handshake
against such a broker fails with `SaslException: Invalid SCRAM server
first message format: r=...,i=٤٠٩٦` (non-Java clients reject it the same
way).

This passes `Locale.ROOT` to that `String.format` call, as already done
for `toLowerCase()` under KAFKA-20638 and for the
`tools`/`server-common` modules under KAFKA-20646 (which does not cover
`clients`), and adds a test that switches the default locale to `ar-EG`
(guarded with `@ResourceLock(Resources.LOCALE)`) and verifies the
message still uses ASCII digits. The other `String.format` calls in
`ScramMessages` only use `%s` and are not locale-sensitive.

Following review, it also removes
`ScramCredentialUtils.credentialToString()` / `credentialFromString()`:
the ZooKeeper-era credential string format had the same `%d` problem but
no callers left outside its own tests, so the methods, their constants
and the tests that only exercised them are gone.
`ScramCredentialUtils.createCache()` and its test are unchanged.

Reproduced against the released `kafka-clients` 4.4.0 jar on JDK 25:
```
java -Duser.language=ar -Duser.country=EG ...
server-first-message on the wire =
r=clientnonceservernonce,s=MDEy...,i=٤٠٩٦
client parse                     = FAILED: Invalid SCRAM server first
message format
```

KAFKA-21230: Pause processing on uncommitted bytes (#23728)

During a long rebalance, a `StreamThread` can use native memory without
limit and fail with an out-of-memory error. When the uncommitted state
store bytes exceed `statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes`,
`StreamThread#maybeCommit` forces a commit. But `TaskManager` skips
commits during a rebalance, and `runOnceWithoutProcessingThreads`
continues to process records. Thus the uncommitted bytes continue to
increase. RocksDB keeps these bytes in a `WriteBatch` in native memory,
outside the block cache and the write buffers.

At the start of each iteration of the processing loop, `StreamThread`
now calls `maybePauseProcessingForUncommittedBytes()`, which checks
`shouldCommitDueToUncommittedBytes()`. Because `maybeCommit` commits at
the end of each iteration, the bytes exceed the limit at this point only
when that commit was skipped or failed. So the check needs no extra
state. While processing is paused, the thread does not process records
or run punctuators, because both write to the state stores. It continues
to poll, so the rebalance can complete, and it continues to call
`maybeCommit`. Processing resumes when a commit succeeds, or when a
commit on partition revocation flushes the buffers. The thread logs the
pause and the resume at INFO level.

This change decreases throughput during a long rebalance, but it
prevents the out-of-memory error. `GlobalStreamThread` does not need
this change, because one thread writes to its stores, checks the bytes
and flushes them, and nothing skips that flush. A separate pull request
will apply the same pause to processing threads.

Two new `StreamThreadTest` tests cover the change.
`shouldNotProcessOrPunctuateWhileUncommittedBytesExceedLimit` shows that
the thread polls and tries to commit, but does not process or punctuate,
while the commit is skipped.
`shouldResumeProcessingOnceUncommittedBytesAreCommitted` shows that
processing stays paused for the iteration in which the rebalance
completes, and resumes only after the commit succeeds.

KAFKA-21344: Handle partition rotation for share fetches (#23951)

A share fetch hands its record budget to partitions in the order they
are read, so the partition read first  takes the largest share. Two
things decided that order earlier and together they could starve a
partition, hence changed the behaviour.

Earlier:
- `SharePartitionManager` rotated the fetch list by `sessionEpoch %
size`. The client bumps the epoch on both
  ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge, so in a poll-and-commit loop fetch
epochs step by two and the rotation is
  constant. One unpaired request flips the parity, and with two
partitions the rotation then undoes the
  session reorder on every fetch, so the same partition is read first
until the other starves.
- `ShareSessionContext` moved served partitions to the end of the
session from inside the response iterator,
  in the iteration order of the response map. That map had passed
through `HashMap` copies, so when every
  partition returned records the session ended up in hash order and the
same partition led every fetch.

PR:

This change removes the epoch rotation from the fetch path and makes the
session reorder deterministic from  the fetch order. The fetch order is
preserved through `ShareFetchUtils`, `ShareFetch` and `KafkaApis` with
`LinkedHashMap`s. `ShareSessionContext` reorders the session in one pass
before pruning the response:  partitions without records keep their
position at the front, and partitions with records are appended in fetch
order rotated by one, so the partition read first is read last next
time. `PartitionRotateStrategy`  is reduced to that rotation and the
unused `sessionEpoch` parameter of `fetchMessages` is dropped.

`ShareConsumerFairnessTest` adds cases for the epoch parity change, for
the first position rotating when all partitions return records with
explicit and implicit acknowledgement, and for an idle partition being
read first once it has records.

`SharePartitionManagerTest` verifies the session order across subsequent
fetches.

KAFKA-21234: FileRecords#readInto should honor slice boundaries (#23737)

When the metadata layer (e.g. MetadataLoader) tries to read a slice of
records from KRaft which is greater than
KafkaRaftClient#MAX_BATCH_SIZE_BYTES, the RecordsIterator can return
records which are past the slice (HWM). As it iterates through this
slice of
records, FileRecords#readInto reads from disk the minimum of the bytes
until end of the file and the remaining space in the associated buffer.
In the case of the former, this can lead to a metadata error where the
node tries to snapshot with records past the HWM.

For the metadata error to occur, the following three pre-conditions must
be met:

1. One committed read handed to a listener is larger than 8 MiB.
2. The segment file has bytes after the HWM, meaning records this node
already appended but that aren't committed yet.
3. For the error to actually show up, the snapshot generator emits a
snapshot from the resulting image before the HWM catches up.

The underlying cause is the same as KAFKA-20841. Thanks to @asdf2014
for working on this issue as part of
https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22963.

Change `FileRecords#readInto` which reads from the underlying file to
the minimum of:

1. The remaining space in the associated buffer, which in the case of
RecordsIterator is the minimum of the FileRecords' record size and
the batch size defined by KRaft.
2. The end byte position of the FileRecords object, rather than the end
of the underlying file. This ensures when a caller constructs a
FileRecords slice of [start position, HWM), no bytes past the HWM are
read into memory.

MINOR: Track share fetch offset metadata per DelayedShareFetch instead of SharePartition (#23911)

DelayedShareFetch estimates the available bytes for minBytes by
comparing the end offset with the cached LogOffsetMetadata of the fetch
offset. The cache was kept on SharePartition, so it outlived the request
which populated it. A partition that is read but trimmed from the
response, or whose request fails, kept a valid cache entry although its
fetch offset did not advance, which requires resets and made the read
path depend on state left behind by earlier requests.

Keep the metadata inside DelayedShareFetch for the lifetime of the
request, as DelayedFetch does with FetchPartitionStatus. The retries of
tryComplete in purgatory still avoid reading from the log, and the cache
can no longer go stale across requests, so the remote fetch reset is not
needed.

backlog are both served under record_limit acquire mode.

There are also cases where if a record is released where it was earlier
fetch then request has to go through timeout to fetch data. Those
scenarios are also handled by this fix.

KAFKA-21214: [7/N] Add the partition placement of the uniform2 assignor (#23736)

The quotas of the uniform2 assignor tell how many partitions of every
topic each member gets. Once the steps have decided them, the assignor
places the partitions.

This patch adds `PartitionPlacement`, which places the partitions of a
topic on its subscribers, moving as few partitions as possible. Every
owner keeps its partitions with the lowest ids, up to its quota. The
other partitions, those without an owner and those beyond the quota of
their owner, go to the subscribers below their quota, each taking the
lowest ids left. A partition thus moves only when its owner owns more
partitions than its quota. `place` returns `false` when every partition
stays with its owner, so that the members keep their current sets of
partitions of the topic.

KAFKA-20404: Replace bulk DefaultStateUpdater atomicity excludes with field-level suppressions (#22333)

## Background
[KAFKA-20404](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20404) tracks
replacing the bulk SpotBugs atomicity excludes (introduced when SpotBugs
was upgraded from 4.8.6 to 4.9.4) with per-field investigations. This PR
handles `DefaultStateUpdater$StateUpdaterThread`, the second class in
the series after `StreamThread` (#22320).

## Investigation
After removing `DefaultStateUpdater$StateUpdaterThread` from the two
bulk excludes it appeared in
(`AT_NONATOMIC_OPERATIONS_ON_SHARED_VARIABLE` at line 505 and
`AT_NONATOMIC_64BIT_PRIMITIVE` at line 544 on trunk), SpotBugs reports
exactly one field with warnings:

- `totalCheckpointLatency` at `DefaultStateUpdater.java:100`, flagged at
line 732 (`measureCheckpointLatency`) and line 750 (`recordMetrics`).

Walking the call sites:
- `measureCheckpointLatency` is `private` and only called from within
`StateUpdaterThread`: `restoreTasks`, `pauseTasks`, `resumeTasks`,
`removeUpdatingTask`, `maybeCheckpointTasks`.
- `recordMetrics` is `private` and only called from
`StateUpdaterThread.runOnce` (line 213).
- All callers run on the `StateUpdaterThread` itself (the inner class
extends `Thread`).

So `totalCheckpointLatency` is thread-confined and the SpotBugs warnings
are false positives.

## Changes
- Remove `DefaultStateUpdater$StateUpdaterThread` from the two bulk
`<Or>` blocks.
- Add two targeted `<Match>` blocks scoped to the class plus the
`totalCheckpointLatency` field, each with a rationale comment explaining
the thread-confinement, one per bug pattern.

## Verification
- `:streams:spotbugsMain --rerun-tasks` clean.
- `:streams:checkstyleMain` / `:streams:checkstyleTest` /
`:streams:spotbugsTest` clean.
- `:streams:test --tests "*DefaultStateUpdater*"` all green.

KAFKA-21280: Do not send stale bytes after a failed file read in SslTransportLayer.transferFrom (#23832)

`SslTransportLayer.transferFrom` clears `fileChannelBuffer` before
reading the next chunk of the file. When the read threw, or returned no
bytes, the buffer was left cleared rather than flipped, so it still
looked full of the previous chunk. If bytes had already been written in
the same call the `IOException` was swallowed, and the next call sent
the stale buffer as the contents of the position that could not be read:
a read error on the segment never surfaced, and the client received a
corrupt batch.

This flips the buffer whether or not the read succeeds, so that it holds
exactly what was read: nothing after a failed read or at the end of the
file. It also rethrows the `IOException` when bytes were already written
in the same call: the connection is closed on it anyway, and returning
the bytes written only delayed the error to the next call.

KAFKA-16304: Offline the log directory on a disk error in the zero-copy Fetch path (#23445)

The Fetch response is sent zero copy: the records are read from the
segment by `FileRecords.writeTo`, on the network thread, while the
response is written to the socket. A failed read of the medium and a
client that went away both arrive there as a bare `IOException`, and
`Selector` treats every one of them as a disconnect. A disk error on
this path therefore never offlines the log directory, unlike an I/O
error in the `LocalLog` operations.

This change offlines it, with the same split as elsewhere in the log:
the layer that sees the `IOException` reports it, and storage decides.

* `LocalLog.read` gives the `FileRecords` slices it returns a transfer
  failure handler.
* When the transfer fails, `FileRecords.writeTo` passes the region it
  was writing to the handler and rethrows the original exception
  unchanged. A `ClosedChannelException` is not passed on: the file was
  not read.
* The handler re-reads the region on the log's scheduler, at most once
  at a time per log directory, and calls
  `LogDirFailureChannel.maybeAddOfflineLogDir` only if the read fails,
  with the failed transfer attached. As the log cleaner does, the
  directory is offlined and the error is not rethrown.

The network thread does no extra I/O on a failed send. The send itself
is logged as a disconnect, at DEBUG; the ERROR comes from
`LogDirFailureChannel`.

The classification is as accurate as what the JVM reports, and no more.
Nothing below the JVM is second-guessed: a transient media error that
has cleared by the time of the re-read is attributed to the socket, and
a read that fails for a reason other than the medium is treated as a
storage failure, the criterion `LocalLog` already applies. At the JVM
level, the re-read of the region:

* reads completely: the socket was at fault;
* reaches the end of the file: the log was truncated concurrently (e.g.
  the replica became a follower);
* makes no progress: nothing can be concluded;
* fails with `ClosedChannelException` or a subclass: the segment was
  closed or deleted concurrently, which says nothing about the medium
  (the reasoning of KAFKA-19571);
* fails with any other `IOException`: the log directory is offlined.

The whole region is re-read rather than its first byte because,
depending on the platform, the transfer can fail anywhere within it
without reporting progress: on macOS both `sendfile(2)` and `read(2)`
drop the partial progress of a chunk whose read fails, and on Windows
the JDK does not use `TransmitFile` for a non-blocking socket and falls
back to a mapped buffer or `ReadFile`. On Linux the transfer fails at
the first unreadable page. The re-read reads at most what the failed
call was about to send. The message text of the exception is not
inspected: it is platform specific.

Once the directory is offline its segments are closed, and the next
Fetch gets `KAFKA_STORAGE_ERROR`.

Consequences worth stating:

* A broker whose only log directory, or whose metadata log directory,
  fails on this path now shuts down, as it does today for any other I/O
  error in that directory.
* The KRaft metadata log is read through `LocalLog` too. A read failure
  while the leader sends it marks the raft log's directory offline, the
  next append on the leader fails, and the raft I/O thread's fatal fault
  handler stops the node, as it does today for an I/O error in
  `LocalLog.read` on the metadata log.

KAFKA-21181: Allow committing an empty transaction in TV2 (#23831)

Follow-up to #23630, addressing
https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23630#discussion_r4151983373.
#23630
returns NOT_COORDINATOR once the broker has applied the leadership
change;
this covers a coordinator whose metadata is still behind.

With transaction V2, an EndTxn(COMMIT) at the current epoch on a
transaction
in Empty, CompleteCommit or CompleteAbort state returned
INVALID_TXN_STATE,
which is fatal to the client. A coordinator that has lost leadership but
not
yet applied the metadata change sees the transaction in exactly this
state,
since its partitions were added on the new coordinator, and answered
from its
stale cache.

Commit an empty transaction instead, the same way an empty abort is
handled:
bump the epoch, write PrepareCommit with no partitions and complete it
without
markers.

- A stale coordinator cannot get that write replicated. The transaction
log
is written with acks=-1, and the new leader is in the old leader's ISR
but
stopped fetching from it before the partitions were added. The client
gets
a retriable error (NOT_COORDINATOR or COORDINATOR_NOT_AVAILABLE), looks
up
  the coordinator again and commits on the new one.
- A coordinator that is up to date only sees an empty transaction when
the
client wrote nothing, since a TV2 produce always adds its partition to
the
  transaction before it succeeds. Committing it is a no-op epoch bump.

Retries are unchanged: CompleteCommit + Commit + Retry still returns
NONE and
CompleteAbort + Commit + Retry still returns PRODUCER_FENCED.
Transaction V1
is unchanged. A PrepareCommit with no partitions is loaded and completed
the
same way as the empty PrepareAbort that TV2 already writes.

Tests cover the updated state table, completing without markers, the
retriable error when the write fails, producer ID rotation on an
exhausted
epoch, and loading an empty PrepareCommit from the log.

KAFKA-20999: [1/N] Add RackAwareStandbyPicker for rack-aware standby placement (#23790)

First part of rack-aware standby placement for streams groups. It adds
RackAwareStandbyPicker, which the sticky assignor and balanced assignor
will use to place standbys by rack.aware.assignment.tags. Nothing calls
it yet; the next PR wires it into StickyTaskAssignor.

A process meets a tag key when it has a value for it that no holder of
the task has yet. For the next standby of a task, pick() chooses the
conditions: every tag key with an unused value if a process with room
meets them all; otherwise, the tag keys in configured order, each kept
only if a process with room still meets it together with those kept so
far. It returns the conditions together with the least-loaded process
with room that meets them, or null once no process with room can make
the task more diverse.

The processes sit in a tree with one level per tag key, so a pick does
not scan every combination of tag values. Each node keeps the
least-loaded process with room below it, and its children are ordered by
it. The caller reports load and room changes with updated() and
updatedAll(), which repair only the affected paths.

KAFKA-21214: [6/N] Add the balance step of the uniform2 assignor (#23735)

uniform2 decides how many partitions of every topic each member gets,
its quotas, in three steps. The first two give every extra partition to
a distinct subscriber of its topic, but they can leave a member with an
assignment much larger than another subscriber of one of its topics.

This patch adds the balance step, `BalanceExtraPartitions`, which the
assignor runs after the other two steps in a later patch. The step
applies a single rule until it no longer applies. The member with the
largest assignment, among those with an extra partition that can move,
gives one to the smallest member that can take it, which is a subscriber
of the topic, with no extra partition of the topic and at least two
partitions smaller. Every move lowers the sum of the squares of the
assignment sizes, so the step ends, and it ends exactly when no extra
partition can move to a subscriber of its topic at least two partitions
smaller.

Changes:
- The givers wait in a heap, the largest first, and a giver without a
  receiver is parked until a move may give it one. The step ends once
  the largest giver is less than two partitions above the smallest
  member.
- The giver gives the extra partition whose move revokes the fewest
  partitions. On equal assignment sizes, a giver with a free extra
  partition gives first, and a receiver owning more than the minimum
  quota of a topic with extra partitions receives first, since only
  such a receiver can keep one more of its partitions.
- To find receivers quickly, each giver counts its extra partitions per
  cohort, for the topics that the cohort subscribes to. The counts are
  kept for every member when they fit, and otherwise for one member at
  a time. A constructor forces either way, and a test checks that both
  give the same quotas on random groups.
- When all assignment sizes are within one of each other, nothing can
  move, and the step returns without building any state.

KAFKA-14302: Advance restored offsets after changelog catch-up (#23298)

## What is the bug?

When restoring an empty changelog with a non-zero end offset,
ProcessorStateManager does not update the restored offset because no
records are applied.

As a result, changelogOffsets() can report 0 even though restoration has
completed at a higher offset. This can cause Kafka Streams to
incorrectly report recovery lag for the task.

## What does this change do?

The fix advances the restored offset once changelog restoration has
actually reached its known boundary.

The implementation preserves the existing offset semantics and ensures
that the restored offset does not move backwards.

## Testing

Added regression coverage for:

* An empty changelog with a high end offset.
* Task lag calculation after changelog restoration.
* Active and standby restore scenarios.

Existing relevant Streams tests also pass.

Reviewers: Alan Lau (github:alanlau28), Bill Bejeck <bbejeck@apache.org>

KAFKA-21253: Always clear record collector offsets in closeDirty (#23791)

`RecordCollectorImpl.closeDirty()` aborts the open transaction before
calling `close()`, which clears the collector's changelog offsets. If
the abort throws, `close()` is skipped and the offsets are kept. This
happens with an `IllegalStateException` after a timed-out
`commitTransaction()`. The revived task reuses the collector, so if it
is closed clean while its wiped store is still restoring, those stale
offsets are checkpointed. The next restore then skips the missing
records.

This change moves `close()` into a `finally` block so the offsets are
always cleared. It also logs the abort failure at ERROR before
rethrowing. The caller still swallows the exception, and before this
change it was only logged at DEBUG, without the exception.

`CommitTimeoutDirtyCloseIntegrationTest` uses the fault proxy to
reproduce this. A delayed EndTxn leaves a commit pending, so the abort
fails. A later `ILLEGAL_GENERATION` on `TxnOffsetCommit` migrates the
thread, and the restoring task is closed clean.

The associated integration test replicates the issue and without the fix
in this PR it fails.

KAFKA-21111 [2/N]: Grant tasks at once to members that cannot be warmed up (#23784)

This is the second change of the series that makes the warm-up task
refiner (KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of
the streams group heartbeat (see KAFKA-21111), on top of #23761.

A warm-up task can only complete a migration if the coordinator observes
the target owner restoring it, which a member that heartbeats with
version 0 never allows, as it does not report task offsets. When the
target assignment moves a stateful task to such a member, the refiner no
longer stages the migration. It lets the target assignment through for
that task, so the current owner revokes it and the target owner takes it
over, as it would without a refiner.

The check sits after the readiness check, so that a move between two
members of one process still happens inside the instance, and before the
analysis of the incumbent and of the copies, so that a caught-up copy on
another process is not promoted as a temporary owner. That detour would
only postpone the same cold grant and add a second hand-over. The
version of the current owner is irrelevant: a member that processes a
task is hot by definition, and keeps it while a target owner that can be
warmed up restores it. If the target owner already holds a standby task
of the task, the client recycles it into the active task, so the grant
is warm in the common case, even though the coordinator cannot see that.

The refiner is not the default yet, so this change is not live. The
tests cover the grant, the missing detour through a caught-up copy, and
a current owner of version 0 that keeps its task.

KAFKA-21214: [3/N] Add the quotas and the first two steps of the uniform2 assignor (#23733)

uniform2 decides how many partitions of every topic each member gets,
its quotas, in three steps, and then places the partitions. A topic with
P partitions and N subscribers has a minimum quota of P / N partitions,
and its P % N extra partitions go to as many distinct subscribers.

This patch adds the quotas and their first two steps:
- `Quotas` holds the minimum quota and the extra partitions of every
  topic, the members getting the extra partitions, and the assignment
  sizes of the members. The steps give the extra partitions and move
  them.
- `KeepStickyExtraPartitions`: a member owning more than the minimum
  quota of a topic keeps one of its extra partitions, the members with
  the smallest assignments first when the owners outnumber the extra
  partitions.
- `AssignRemainingExtraPartitions` gives the extra partitions that
  nobody kept, one at a time, to subscribers without one of the topic,
  among the ones with the smallest assignments: the topics with the
  fewest subscribers first, and round robin within a cohort. It returns
  without allocating anything when the owners kept them all.
- `IntPair` packs two ints in a long, so that pairs sort in a `long[]`
  or a `LongHeap` without allocating.
- A step is created with what it works on and run once; the assignor
  runs the steps in order in a later patch.
- `QuotasFixture` holds the indexed group, the current assignment and
  the quotas of a group for the tests of the steps.

The balance step comes in a later patch.

KAFKA-21194 [1/N]: Place active tasks with the Sainte-Laguë method in the balanced assignor (#23755)

The balanced task assignor placed stateful active tasks round-robin over
the processes and then ran a fix-up loop that moves tasks between
processes while a move reduces the skew of the per-member load. Every
pass of that loop tests all pairs of processes, so it costs O(P^2) per
pass even when nothing moves.

This deals the active tasks with the Sainte-Laguë divisor method
instead: in sorted task order, each task goes to the process with the
smallest (2n + 1) / c, where n is the number of tasks the process holds
so far and c its number of members, ties going to the smaller process
ID. Stateless tasks continue the same sequence after the stateful ones,
instead of going to the process with the lowest active load. The
sequence is periodic, so one period is computed up front and each task
is then a lookup.

- With equal member counts the deal is round-robin, so the placement is
  unchanged.
- With unequal member counts the per-member loads of any two processes
  still differ by at most one, and no move of the old fix-up loop would
  change the placement. Each subtopology is now spread over the
  processes nearly in proportion to their member counts, where the loop
  could leave most of a subtopology on one process.

Standby placement is unchanged.

Testing: the existing `BalancedTaskAssignorTest` cases pass, and a new
case checks that each subtopology is split two to one between a process
with two members and a process with one.

Benchmark (JMH, full assignment of 1000 members, 100 subtopologies of
100 partitions with every second one stateful, 3 forks, ms per
assignment; before is trunk):

| processes | standbys | before | after | speed-up | sticky |
|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1000 x 1 member | 0 | 9.06 | 1.65 | 5.5x |
2.96 | | 1000 x 1 member | 1 | 17.09 | 10.19 | 1.7x | 4.70 | | 20 x 50
members | 0 | 2.34 | 1.74 | 1.3x | 2.83 | | 20 x 50 members | 1 | 5.05 |
4.34 | 1.2x | 5.14 | | 400 of 1-4 members | 0 | 17.29 | 1.68 | 10.3x |
3.30 | | 400 of 1-4 members | 1 | 20.92 | 4.36 | 4.8x | 4.68 |

With standbys most of the remaining time is the unchanged standby
placement, which still runs the fix-up loop over all pairs of processes.

KAFKA-21212: Fix rack ID removal on Streams static member rejoin. (#23705)

Fixes KAFKA-21212

When a Streams static member restarted after removing `client.rack`, the
coordinator retained the previous rack ID. During static member
replacement, the coordinator copies the previous member’s metadata, then
applies the incoming updates. Because `maybeUpdateRackId` treats null as
unchanged, the joining request could not clear the copied rack ID. This
left stale rack information in group descriptions and custom assignor
inputs.

This change distinguishes joining requests from regular heartbeats,
following the existing handling of `userEndpoint`. Joining requests now
apply the rack ID directly, including null to clear the previous value.
Regular heartbeats continue to preserve the existing rack ID when the
field is omitted. Clearing a previously configured rack ID also allows
the existing metadata change detection to bump the group epoch and
trigger assignment recomputation.

KAFKA-21111 [1/N]: Tell the refiner which members may be given a warm-up task (#23761)

This is the first change of a series that makes the warm-up task refiner
(KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of the
streams group heartbeat (4.2 and 4.3), and with a coordinator failover
during which the coordinator does not know the version of any member. A
warm-up task is only useful if the coordinator can observe how far its
holder has restored it, which a member reports through the task offsets
of a version 1 heartbeat. A version 0 member never does, so it could
never be promoted from warm-up to active.

This change only provides the information, and nothing uses it yet. The
coordinator records the version of every member's last heartbeat as
transient state of the streams group, with the same lifecycle as the
reported task offsets: written in the heartbeat path, dropped when the
member is removed, and not known again after a coordinator failover
until the member heartbeats. It is deliberately not persisted, so that
it can never outlive the client that sent it. The refiner is handed an
immutable view of it, and decides itself which versions it can warm up.
A member that is missing from the map, because the coordinator has not
heard from the member since it loaded the group, has an unknown version.
The refiner ignores the new input for now; the following changes of this
series use it.

See https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21111. The tests cover
the group state and the versions reaching the refiner through the
heartbeat path.

KAFKA-21214: [2/N] Add the indexed group of the uniform2 assignor (#23732)

The uniform assignor balances the total number of partitions per member
but not the partitions of each topic: with homogeneous subscriptions, a
member can get all the partitions of a topic while the others get none
of them. uniform2, the next version of the uniform assignor, spreads
every topic over its subscribers. It reads the group, decides how many
partitions of every topic each member gets, its quotas, in three steps,
and then places the partitions. This stack adds it one step at a time,
and the assignor itself last.

This patch adds the indexed group that every step reads:
- `IndexedGroup` numbers the members in member id order and the topics
  in topic id order, so that the assignment is deterministic. It drops
  the topics that do not exist, and groups the members with the same
  subscription into cohorts.
- `CurrentAssignment` reads the owner of every partition. What the
  members hold of topics they do not subscribe to, or which no longer
  exist, is stale and dropped.
- `GroupSpecFixture` and `TopicsFixture` build the inputs of the tests.

MINOR: Add warm-up tests for coordinator failover, owner departure and multi-threaded members (#23675)

This adds three warm-up task lifecycle tests for situations that only
arise with real clients and brokers, using the harness from #23620. The
first fails the group coordinator over while a warm-up task is in
flight. The intermediate assignment and the reported offsets are held in
memory only, so the new coordinator derives the intermediate assignment
again from the persisted assignments, and the warm-up task has to
survive that without being closed and restored again, and be promoted
with nothing left to restore. The second has the active owner leave
while the warm-up task is still behind, so the task is handed to the
warm-up task's member right away, and the active task has to continue
restoring from exactly where the warm-up task stopped rather than from
the start. The third runs a member with two stream threads that each
warm up and take over a task, and then removes one thread, after which
the remaining thread restores the moved task from scratch, which is the
current behaviour for in-memory stores until KAFKA-21090.

The multi-threaded test tracks when each task's store is opened and
closed and on which thread, and checks that a process never holds a task
on two threads at once. The published thread metadata cannot be used for
this, since a thread only refreshes it when it starts running again, so
a shutting-down thread keeps listing tasks it has already closed, and a
thread that finished restoring a task since it last started running does
not list it yet.

The cluster runs three brokers with replicated internal topics so that
the coordinator can fail over. The failover test picks an application ID
whose coordinator is not on the broker that also runs the controller, so
that restarting it does not take the metadata quorum down.
EmbeddedKafkaCluster gains a way to restart a broker and to tell which
nodes run the controller.

The tests passed repeated local runs, and the owner-leaves test fails
when the reconciler routes a warm-up promotion through revocation
instead of promoting the warm-up task in place.

KAFKA-21158: Document retention impact of future timestamps allowed by message.timestamp.after.max.ms (#23596)

Ref : https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21158

Follow-up to KAFKA-20609 (#22873), based on review feedback:
https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22873#discussion_r4097159048

Time-based retention is measured from a segment's largest record
timestamp, so a segment holding a record with a future timestamp can't
be deleted by time until that timestamp plus the retention time has
passed.

This applies whether or not tiered storage is used.   Using
`message.timestamp.after.max.ms` limits how far in the future a
timestamp can be.

Changes :
- Document this in the `message.timestamp.after.max.ms` and
`log.message.timestamp.after.max.ms` config docs.
- Log a WARN when the effective value is above the default (1h). Nothing
is rejected and retention behavior is unchanged.

Warnings are fired in 4 places.
- Topic created with its own message.timestamp.after.max.ms in broker
- Topic config altered in broker
- Broker startup in LogManager
- Broker config changed in runtime in
LogManager.reconfigureDefaultLogConfig

KAFKA-21026: Add JMH benchmark for the streams assignment refiner (#23616)

The streams group coordinator refines the task assignor's target
assignment into an intermediate assignment that holds stateful task
migrations back behind warm-up tasks (KAFKA-20665). The refinement runs
on the heartbeat path: for a stable group, `streamsGroupHeartbeat`
derives it for the whole group on every heartbeat, so its cost scales
with each group's heartbeat rate. This adds a JMH benchmark for it.

`AssignmentRefinerBenchmark` measures one `AssignmentRefiner#refine`
call followed by the `preservesActiveTaskCount` check the coordinator
applies to the result, for `NoOpAssignmentRefiner` (the broker default)
and `AssignmentRefinerImpl`. It calls the public `refine`, so it needs
no change as the refiner evolves. The group is set up as a refinement
step finds it: the target assignment comes from the sticky assignor, a
fraction of the stateful active tasks still runs on a member of another
process, the warm-up budget is already spent on migrations under way,
and the members report restore progress according to a lag picture (all
caught up, all lagging, not reported, mixed, or destinations that are
themselves restoring an active task). The parameters cover member count,
members per process, subtopology and partition count, standby replicas,
the warm-up budget, the migrating fraction and the lag picture. The
default grid is trimmed to values that bracket the behaviour; the rest
are reachable with `-p`.

`StreamsAssignorBenchmarkUtils` gains the two fixture builders this
needs: `divergeAssignment`, which derives the members' current
assignment from the target, and `createMemberTaskOffsets`, which builds
the offsets and end offsets the members report in their heartbeats.

Testing: `./gradlew :jmh-benchmarks:compileJava checkstyleMain
spotbugsMain` passes. A probe over the fixtures confirmed that no
process ever holds two copies of a task, that the active task count is
preserved, and that each lag picture drives a different refiner decision
(grant, keep, plant, park). A run against trunk with the refiner wired
in (288 refiner rows, 5 warm-up and 5 measured iterations of 1 s) shows
that a stable group with nothing to move is the dominant cost: about
4.2-4.8 ms and 5 MB per call at 5,000 stateful tasks with one standby,
58-111 times the no-op refiner, largely independent of member count.
Moving half of the stateful tasks adds 50-100% on top, and the warm-up
budget (2 vs. 100) makes no measurable difference.

MINOR: Add broker integration tests for classic JoinGroup topology cleanup (#23747)

Converting an empty streams group to a classic group requires the broker
to delete the group's stored topology description from the plugin first.
This path was only unit-tested against mocks; no test sent a real
classic JoinGroupRequest to a running broker, and the failed-join and
periodic-cleanup halves were never chained together.

StreamsGroupTopologyDescriptionRequestTest. The first joins a classic
member to an empty streams group with a stored topology and checks that
the broker calls plugin.deleteTopology and converts the group. The

replays to the defaults. Before, it replayed to
an empty map, which never equaled the current configs, so every such
group rebalanced once after the broker
upgrade. Now it only rebalances if a current config differs from its
default.                                                             -

- `GroupAssignment` copies its member map with `Map.copyOf`, so
`members()` is unmodifiable and null keys or
values are rejected.

KAFKA-21088: Restore PUSH_NEEDED when telemetry payload construction fails (#23590)

[KAFKA-21088](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21088)

`DefaultClientTelemetrySender.createPushRequest` moves the sender to
`PUSH_IN_PROGRESS` before the payload is assembled. When assembly threw,
the
catch block logged a warning, called `updateErrorResult` and returned
`Optional.empty()` without restoring the state. No request was sent, so
neither
`handleResponse` nor `handleFailedRequest` could run to move the sender
on, and
`timeToNextUpdate` returns `requestTimeoutMs` for `PUSH_IN_PROGRESS`, so
`NetworkClient.TelemetrySender.maybeUpdate` never called
`createRequest()`
again. Telemetry stopped for the lifetime of the client after a single
WARN,
while the sender still reported itself as enabled.

This restores `PUSH_NEEDED` for a non-terminating push, so the retry on
the next
push interval that the existing comment describes actually happens. A
terminating push is left alone: `TERMINATING_PUSH_IN_PROGRESS` can only
transition to `TERMINATED`, and `close()` follows it, so it is not a
stuck
state. Attempting the transition there would fail `validateTransition`
and
disable telemetry as a side effect.

### Testing

Two tests in `ClientTelemetryReporterTest`, both using a mocked
`KafkaMetricsCollector` whose `collect` throws:

- `testCreateRequestPushPayloadFailureRetriesOnNextInterval` asserts the
sender
lands in `PUSH_NEEDED`, that `timeToNextUpdate` returns the push
interval
rather than the request timeout, and that a `PushTelemetryRequest` is
built
  once the interval elapses.
- `testCreateRequestTerminatingPushPayloadFailure` asserts the
terminating path
stays in `TERMINATING_PUSH_IN_PROGRESS` with telemetry still enabled,
and that
  `close()` reaches `TERMINATED`.

Both fail against the unfixed code (`expected: <PUSH_NEEDED> but was:
<PUSH_IN_PROGRESS>`). `clients:spotlessCheck`, `checkstyleMain` and
`checkstyleTest` pass.

MINOR: Add streams group integration tests for the warm-up task lifecycle (#23620)

This extends the end-to-end coverage of warm-up tasks under the streams
group protocol beyond the scale-out case in #23608, with real Kafka
Streams clients against the real AssignmentRefinerImpl. The tests cover
the warm-up budget when two members join at once (only one migration is
warmed up while the other waits, and the waiting one is warmed up rather
than moved cold once the budget frees), and the scale-in mirror of
#23608, where a member leaving makes the target assignment no longer
want an in-flight warm-up task, which is then given up while its owner
keeps running the task. Warm-up revocation was so far only verified at
the coordinator level. They also cover the client reporting a warm-up
task's offsets on the next heartbeat once it is caught up, even with a
task offset interval far longer than the test, promotion being gated on
acceptable.recovery.lag (withheld at a known lag above the threshold,
promoted once the threshold is raised while the lag is held constant),
and tasks moving cold with no warm-up task when num.warmup.replicas is
0.

Where a test has to hold a warm-up task behind, the instance's restore
consumer, which unlike the main consumer is still taken from the client
supplier under the streams group protocol, lets a small budget of
records through and then withholds the rest. A budget is needed rather
than a gate that is closed from the start, since a warm-up task that has
restored nothing reports no offset, and there would be no lag to gate
on. EmbeddedKafkaCluster gains setters for the warm-up related group
configs, and setGroupHeartbeatTimeout is renamed to
setGroupHeartbeatInterval, since it sets streams.heartbeat.interval.ms
and the old name suggested a timeout.

The tests surfaced that a client reports an active task's restore having
finished only with its next offset report, which can be up to
streams.task.offset.interval.ms later, and that until then the refiner
takes the owner to still be restoring and moves the task without warming
it up. The tests therefore run with the shortest task offset interval
and wait for the broker to see all active tasks running before staging a
migration.

Tests for coordinator failover, the active owner leaving mid-warm-up,
and members with several stream threads follow in a separate PR stacked
on this one.

The test class passed repeated local runs (20 consecutive runs before
the split, with one failure traced to a race in the test itself and
fixed). Each key assertion was also checked against a mutation that
should break it: disabling the client's hot warm-up report trigger,
making isCaughtUp ignore the threshold, and making the refiner ignore
the warm-up budget each make the corresponding test fail.

MINOR: Avoid a lambda allocation per lookup in CachedTopicResolver (#23710)

`CachedTopicResolver.id` and `CachedTopicResolver.name` pass a lambda
capturing the key to `HashMap.computeIfAbsent`, so every lookup
allocates one, cache hits included. The JIT does not eliminate it:
`HashMap.computeIfAbsent` is above C2's inlining limit, so the lambda
escapes. `TopicIds` calls `id` for every topic it iterates and `name` in
`contains`, so an assignor walking the subscriptions of a heterogeneous
group allocates one lambda per member and subscribed topic.

calls `put` on a miss. As before, an unknown topic resolves to `null`
and is not cached. It also adds `topicId` and `topicName` to

KAFKA-21196: Release memory held by cancelled CoordinatorExecutorImpl tasks (#23674)

When a `CoordinatorExecutorImpl` task is cancelled, it remains in the
executor queue or in the event processor queue until it is processed and
it retains its runnable, its operation and the result of its runnable in
the meantime. When the group coordinator is overloaded, these queues can
grow large and retain data structures that are no longer needed, e.g.
the metadata image captured by the regular expression resolution.

This patch boxes the runnable, the operation and the result in a `Task`
object which releases them when the task is cancelled. The operation and
the result are also released once the operation is executed because the
write event is retained until its records are committed.

MINOR: Add streams group protocol integration test for warm-up tasks (#23608)

This ports the scale-out warm-up scenario from
HighAvailabilityTaskAssignorIntegrationTest, which exercises the classic
protocol's client-side HighAvailabilityTaskAssignor, to the streams
group protocol. Under the streams group protocol, warm-up derivation
happens broker-side via an AssignmentRefiner, which defaults to a no-op
implementation, so the test enables the real AssignmentRefinerImpl
explicitly to get coverage of the actual warm-up behavior against a live
cluster with real KafkaStreams clients, which did not exist before.

The test proves the same property as the original: when a stateful app
scales out, the new instance is first handed a warm-up task rather than
being promoted to active immediately, and is only promoted once its
local state has caught up, at which point the promotion happens with
zero real state restoration because the warm-up's state is reused
directly.

Two mechanisms from the original test don't carry over and needed
replacements. There is no client-side assignment-listener equivalent
under the streams group protocol, since that callback is wired into the
classic protocol's client-side assignor, so warm-up assignment and later
promotion are instead detected by polling
KafkaStreams.metadataForLocalThreads() for a task moving from the
standby set into the active set. On the target-assignment side, the
streams group protocol currently only ships the sticky assignor, which
balances active task load across processes rather than doing plain round
robin, but its load-balancing quota math still forces one of the two
tasks in this scenario onto the new, empty instance's target assignment,
which is exactly the mismatch the refiner needs in order to stage a
warm-up. So the test works with the sticky assignor as is, and does not
need to wait for a more round-robin-like assignor.

The rack-aware parameterization from the original test was dropped,
since the streams group protocol's sticky assignor has no rack-aware
placement logic today, so that axis would not exercise anything
meaningful. The in-memory versus persistent store parameterization was
kept, since it is a pure client-side choice orthogonal to the group
protocol.

### Test plan

- Ran both parameterized variants locally against a live 3-broker
embedded KRaft cluster; both pass.
- Confirmed via logs that the new instance is assigned a warm-up task
before promotion (`warm-up tasks {0_1}`, no active task), and that the
state-restore listener reports zero restored records at promotion time.
- `./gradlew spotlessApply checkstyleMain checkstyleTest` is clean.

Reviewers: Bill Bejeck <bbejeck@apache.org>

KAFKA-20998: Add balanced task assignor for streams groups (#23419)

The streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071) ships one built-in task
assignor, "sticky". This adds a second, "balanced", a translation of the
placement in the classic `HighAvailabilityTaskAssignor`:

- Stateful active tasks are dealt round-robin over the processes, then
  moved between processes while a move reduces the per-member load skew.
- Standbys go to the least loaded process that does not hold the task,
  and stateless tasks fill in by active task load.
- Within a process, tasks are spread over its members the way the
  classic client spreads them over its stream threads
  (`assignTasksToThreads`): stateful actives, then standbys, then
  stateless actives, each round levelling the members' task counts. A
  stateful task stays on the member that holds it in any role (active,
  standby or warm-up) where that leaves no other member short.

Reported offsets are not read: warm-up tasks are the assignment
refiner's job (KAFKA-20665), and rack-aware standby placement is
KAFKA-20999. A shortfall of standby replicas is logged once per
assignment at INFO.

The assignor is not registered as a built-in yet, so
`streams.assignor.name=balanced` is still rejected and the docs are
unchanged. Registering it (appending it to
`GroupCoordinatorConfig.STREAMS_GROUP_BUILTIN_ASSIGNORS`) waits for an
optimized implementation, since the all-pairs skew loop takes 6-18 ms
for 1000 single-member processes (up to 25x the sticky assignor), and
for KIP-1071 to be amended from `highly_available` to `balanced`.

Testing: `BalancedTaskAssignorTest` covers distribution across processes
and members, member stickiness within a process (including standbys and
role changes), the standby shortfall, stateless placement, determinism,
and a seeded randomized check over 200 groups asserting validity, the
cross-process fixed point and the per-round levelling.
`StreamsStickyAssignorBenchmark` becomes `StreamsAssignorBenchmark` with
an `assignorType` parameter (run `BALANCED` with `-p
reportedOffsets=NONE`); the balanced assignor takes 1-5x the sticky
assignor's time except at 1000 single-member processes.

KAFKA-20803: Demultiplex batched persister responses once (WriteStateHandler) (#22835)

fix: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20803

PersisterStateManager coalesces many partitions into a single
WRITE_SHARE_GROUP_STATE RPC. On completion, every per-partition handler
re-scanned the full combined response to find its own slice — N handlers
*  O(N) scan = O(N ^ 2 ), all on the single send thread, stalling the
send loop.

This PR demultiplexes the combined response once into a topicId ->
partition -> result index (PartitionResultIndex, built in the send loop
and shared across the handlers of one coalesced request) and  converts
WriteStateHandler to an O(1) lookup.

Scope is deliberately limited to WRITE: it is the hot path, since every
acknowledgement/commit drives a write. readState runs once per
SharePartition lifetime, initializeState once per group-topic-partition,
and delete/read-summary are admin-invoked — for those, building an index
would cost more than the lookup it saves, so they keep the existing
scan.

KAFKA-21161: Checkpoint consumed offset over produced offset for source-topic changelog stores (#23585)

When a task both consumes a source-topic changelog partition (a KTable
that reuses its  source topic as its changelog) and produces to that
same partition, `StreamTask.checkpointableOffsets()`  gave the produced
offset precedence over the consumed offset. On a clean suspend, close,
or  recycle, the store's changelog offset was set to the last offset the
task *wrote*, which can be  ahead of the last offset actually *applied*
to the store. A later restore or standby update  starting from that
checkpoint silently skips the records in between, leaving those keys
stale or  missing — with no error or warning.

KAFKA-20292 [6/N]: Add TargetAssignmentRecordsBuilder (#22487)

To accommodate asynchronous assignors, such as assignors offloaded to
the background thread pool and client-side assignors, we require a
builder to turn a new target assignment into records to be persisted.
Previously, the logic lived within the TargetAssignmentBuilder classes.
We copy the logic out into its own builder class, keeping the existing
logic within the TargetAssignmentBuilders for now.

Future commits will remove the record-building logic from the
TargetAssignmentBuilder classes and update callers to use the new
TargetAssignmentRecordsBuilders.

Additionally, we have to handle concurrent member operations such as
leaves and static member replacements when building the target
assignment records for asynchronous assignors. These member operations
update the target assignment directly. Once the new target assignment is
ready, we have to apply any member operations we missed to it. That is,
we act as if the member removals and static member replacements are
reordered after the assignment calculation.

KAFKA-14405: Log a warning when users attempt to set a config controlled by Streams (#22586)

Kafka Streams assigns some of the underlying consumer and producer
configs itself and silently ignored a user-supplied value for them, so
there was no way to tell that the setting had no effect. Two unrelated
mechanisms did this: a checker driven by the `NON_CONFIGURABLE_*` arrays
that inspected the prefix-extracted user properties, and direct `put()`
calls applied after those properties were merged, which warned about
nothing at all.

Replace both with a single helper, `overwriteControlledConfig`, applied
to  the fully assembled config map so that an override is caught in one
place whichever prefix supplied it, and split the config sets by intent:
`DEFAULT_*` holds defaults the user may still override, `CONTROLLED_*`
holds  values the user cannot. The `_EOS_ONLY` maps carry only what
exactly-once  adds and are applied on top of their counterparts.

This closes two gaps. `group.id` and `partition.assignment.strategy` are
documented as controlled by Streams but produced no log line, because
both are forced with a put() after the merge. The per-client prefixes
were only checked against the non-exactly-once set, so
`restore.consumer.isolation.level=read_uncommitted` gave a restore
consumer reading uncommitted records under exactly-once; it now yields
`read_committed`.

Warnings are now all logged at `WARN`, where the non-exactly-once set
was  previously logged at `ERROR`, and a config that is only controlled
under  exactly-once names the processing guarantee as the reason.

A value that differs from the Streams value only in type, such as
`Boolean.FALSE` where Streams sets `"false"`, no longer warns that it is
being replaced by an identical value.
`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` is a producer config and is now
validated only there, so a value supplied under a consumer prefix is no
longer rejected.

MINOR: Write the streams topology tombstone before the group epoch tombstone (#23552)

Deleting a streams group leaks its topics in the group coordinator's
topic-to-groups index (`groupsByTopics`), which `onMetadataUpdate` uses
to tell groups that a topic they depend on changed.

A streams group's entry in that index is derived from its topology:
replaying a `StreamsGroupTopologyValue` record subscribes the group to
the topology's required topics and replaying its tombstone unsubscribes
it. `StreamsGroup.createGroupTombstoneRecords` wrote the
`StreamsGroupMetadataValue` tombstone before the
`StreamsGroupTopologyValue` tombstone. On replay, the first one removes
the group, so the second one finds no group and returns before
unsubscribing anything. The entry survives for the lifetime of the
coordinator, and every deleted streams group adds to it. The consumer of
the index checks that the group still exists, so the effect is bounded
growth of the index and a spurious metadata refresh request on a group
that later reuses the id, not a failure.

This change writes the topology tombstone before the group epoch
tombstone. This restores the invariant the other group types already
have: every sibling record is torn down before the epoch tombstone, so
the epoch tombstone is the last record of a deletion. Deletions already
in the log with the previous order keep leaking on replay until
compaction removes their tombstones.

The new test builds a streams group with a topology, replays exactly the
records that `createGroupTombstoneRecords` produces, and verifies that
the group is removed and that the index no longer references it. It
fails with the previous record order.

Reviewers: Lucas Brutschy <lbrutschy@confluent.io>

MINOR: Fix static members being fenced by their own instance id (#23542)

A static member that joins with epoch 0 while the coordinator still
considers it active gets UNRELEASED_INSTANCE_ID, which is fatal for the
Java client. This happens when the response to its join is lost or after
a FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH error, because the client keeps its member id and
rejoins with it. A dynamic member in the same situation simply gets its
assignment back.

The root cause is that the coordinator does not enforce that a member id
keeps its instance id. On a join, a known member id may come with any
instance id, so the coordinator cannot tell that the same member is back
and treats it as a replacement of the instance id's owner, itself.

This patch rejects a join that changes the instance id of an existing
member with INVALID_REQUEST. A known member id on a join is then always
the static member owning the instance id, and it is handled in place:
after a leave with epoch -2 its epoch is reset and it is reconciled,
otherwise it gets its current state back like a dynamic member. This
also removes the tombstone-and-rewrite of a member rejoining with its
own id after leaving. Consumer and streams groups are updated alike.

Tests cover every join case for both protocols.

the test only continues after the worker is actually blocked while

MINOR: Moving to atomic update of share sessions on initial epoch (#23510)

ShareSessionCache `.remove` and `.maybeCreateSession` are each
individually synchronized — but as two separate calls, not one atomic
unit. If two connections sent an INITIAL_EPOCH request for the same
(groupId, memberId), *faulty client*, at nearly the same time then both
proceed to create a session. `maybeCreateSession` increments
numMembersPerGroup and numPartitions every time it's called. The
sessions map only ever holds one entry per key (second write overwrites
the first), but the counters had already been bumped twice.

on disconnect, only the connection whose mapping still pointed at a live
session gets to decrement the counters. So numMembersPerGroup for that
group gets stuck above zero forever, which means onGroupEmpty never
fires.

MINOR: Fold the Streams bootstrap resolution guard into the generic client config check (#23497)
MINOR: Add upgrade note for config provider allowlist on dynamic broker configs (#23480)

Bound array and tagged-field allocation in generated message readers

Generated request/response readers sized array and tagged-field
collections directly from the sender-declared count. The existing
check bounds a declared count against the remaining buffer bytes, but
that bound assumes roughly one byte per element; a count that passes
it can still translate into a large initial allocation once elements
are unpacked into Java objects, and tagged-field counts had no
remaining-bytes check at all.

Adds, mirroring the existing array-length guard:
- Initial pre-allocation for array/collection fields is capped at
  MessageUtil.MAX_PREALLOCATED_ARRAY_CAPACITY (1000); a larger
  declared count still parses correctly, growing the collection on
  demand as elements are read.
- A declared array/collection length above
  MessageUtil.MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH (1,000,000) is now rejected up front.
- The tagged-field count for flexible-versioned messages is now
  checked the same way array lengths already are: rejected if
  negative, if it exceeds the remaining bytes, or if it exceeds
  MessageUtil.MAX_TAGGED_FIELD_COUNT (10,000).

New tests cover the pre-allocation cap and hard-length cap on both the
ArrayList and keyed-collection (ImplicitLinkedHashMultiCollection)
branches, at the generator level and in a runtime round-trip, the new
tagged-field guards, and end-to-end RequestContext/RequestHeader cases
using the actual ProduceRequestData (v3) and RequestHeaderData (v2)
production classes at large declared-count magnitudes backed by real
padding bytes, so the pre-existing remaining-bytes check alone would
not reject them and the new hard caps are what's being exercised.

KAFKA-21074: Kafka protocol fault proxy clients fixtures (#23438)

A lightweight Kafka wire-protocol fault-injection proxy for integration
tests. Sit it in front of an EmbeddedKafkaCluster, point any client’s
bootstrap.servers at it, and it can inject error codes, drop
connections, or blackhole a client — decoding/encoding with Kafka’s own
protocol classes so it is correct across every wire version (including
flexible/tagged-field ones), no hand-rolled byte offsets.

Placed in `clients/src/testFixtures` so it is reusable from any module.
This is internal test infrastructure only so it does not require a KIP.

Fault primitives, each armed with a fluent, deterministic trigger:

`injectError(apiKey, Errors)` — stamp an error code onto the matching
response,    re-serialized at the correct wire version. Supported APIs:
`END_TXN`,    `INIT_PRODUCER_ID`, `ADD_OFFSETS_TO_TXN`,
`TXN_OFFSET_COMMIT`, `PRODUCE`, `FETCH`    (extensible by registering a
per-API setter).  `disconnectOn(apiKey)` — drop the connection when the
matching response would return    (models the EOS "commit gap"). Works
on any API.  `delayOn(apiKey, Duration)` — hold back the matching
response to model a slow broker,    isolated to that one connection.
`blackholeClient(clientIdSubstring)` — drop all requests from a targeted
client before    the broker sees them, so the broker evicts it by
session timeout (a reversible,    ungraceful one-node partition). Shared
trigger DSL (`Occurrence`): `once()`, `onCall`, `times`, `everyTime()`,
`withProbability(p)`. The deterministic triggers are safe for
assertions; probability is  chaos-mode only. The proxy never closes
sockets unless a `disconnectOn(...)` rule fires,  so it is not itself a
source of flakiness. Rules can be armed/disarmed live from the test
thread and each returns a handle exposing match/fire counts.

KAFKA-21098: RemoteDeleteLag metrics report a phantom lag that never drains after a leader->follower transition (#23471)

### Summary

`RemoteDeleteLagSegments` / `RemoteDeleteLagBytes` can get latched at a
non-zero value that never drains back to 0 after a partition leader
moves to another broker, even though remote deletion is healthy and no
segment is orphaned in remote storage. It is purely a metrics artifact,
but under frequent leadership movement the broker/cluster aggregate
steps up over time as each affected partition contributes a stuck
residual, producing false-positive "delete lag stuck" alerts.

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21098

### Root cause

The copy path was hardened for this exact race in KAFKA-16948 (reset lag
metrics on becoming follower + guard `recordLagStats` with
`!isCancelled()`), but the delete path never got the equivalent
treatment.

On a leader→follower transition, `onLeadershipChange` runs
`doHandleFollowerPartition` (cancels the `RLMExpirationTask`) and then
`removeRemoteTopicPartitionMetrics` (removes the delete-lag gauges). But
an expiration-pool thread already mid-`cleanupExpiredRemoteLogSegments`
for that partition can call `updateRemoteDeleteLagWith(...)` **after**
the gauge was removed, re-registering it at a non-zero value.
`updateRemoteDeleteLagWith` emits unconditionally — it has no
`!isCancelled()` guard.

Because the same pass then reaches `deleteRemoteLogSegment(..., ignored
-> !isCancelled())`, which returns `false` for the now-cancelled task,
the segment is not deleted by this old leader and the counter is never
decremented back down. The gauge stays pinned until the broker re-leads
the partition and completes a fresh pass, the partition is stopped, or
the broker restarts. The underlying segment is not orphaned — the new
leader independently re-evaluates retention and deletes it.

### Fix

Guard `updateRemoteDeleteLagWith` with `!isCancelled()`, mirroring the
copy path's `recordLagStats`. A cancelled expiration task can no longer
re-register the gauge after `removeRemoteTopicPartitionMetrics` has
cleared it.

Also adds a package-private `rlmExpirationTask` test accessor (like the
existing `rlmCopyTask`) so the behavior can be tested directly.

### Testing

Added `testRemoteDeleteLagResetsToZeroOnBecomingFollower` (mirrors
`testTierLagResetsToZeroOnBecomingFollower` on the copy path). It fails
without the guard (the cancelled task re-registers a non-zero lag) and
passes with it. Existing tiered-storage delete-lag tests remain green.

MINOR: Replace ServerSideAssignorBenchmark with ConsumerAssignorBenchmark (#23491)

ServerSideAssignorBenchmark only covers one shape of consumer group:
topics of equal size, disjoint heterogeneous subscriptions, and a single
incremental event, one member joining. It also derives the number of
partitions per topic from a ratio, which gives topics without partitions
at some grid points, and gives racks to the members but not to the
partition replicas.

This patch replaces it with ConsumerAssignorBenchmark. Its parameters
are independent so that any combination can be selected:
- memberCount, topicCount and partitionCount (the total) replace the
  ratio;
- topology: EQUAL, or SKEWED with a few large topics and many small
  ones;
- subscription: HOMOGENEOUS, HETEROGENEOUS_DISJOINT, or
  HETEROGENEOUS_NESTED where topics are shared by several groups of
  members;
- rack: NONE, or PROVIDED with the members spread over the three racks
  of the brokers and every partition replicated in two of them;
- event: FULL, STABLE, JOIN_ONE, JOIN_MANY, LEAVE_ONE, LEAVE_MANY and
  PARTITIONS_ADDED, the group always having memberCount members when
  the assignment is measured.

The benchmark builds its own cluster metadata and group spec with a
small builder, so AssignorBenchmarkUtils is unchanged. The class
documentation describes the parameters and gives the runs to use for
reports.
